lines: Good afternoon, Riverside Cycling Club. This is Helen speaking. How can I help?
Hello. I’m calling because I’m interested in joining the club. I’ve recently moved to the area and I’d like to find out what sort of rides you organise, and what membership costs.

Of course. We have three types of membership. The first is our full membership, which is for people who want to join regular rides and use the club’s workshop. That’s forty-eight pounds a year. We also have a social membership for people who mainly come to events and meetings.
That one is twenty-six pounds annually.
Right. I’m not sure I’d use the workshop, but I would like to go on rides. Is there a cheaper option for someone who hasn’t cycled with a group before?

Yes, we offer a beginner membership. It’s thirty-four pounds for the first year. It includes the group rides, but not workshop access. You can move to full membership later if you decide you’d like to use the workshop.
The beginner option is quite popular with people who are new to cycling in a group.
That sounds suitable. I’ve been cycling on my own for a while, but I haven’t done much group riding. Could you tell me when the club meets?

We have a short ride on Tuesday evenings, but that’s arranged by one of our smaller groups and it isn’t a regular club meeting. Our main meeting is on Thursday. Members meet at the clubhouse at half past six, and the ride usually starts at seven.
Thursday would be fine. Is the meeting every week?

Yes, every Thursday, except for public holidays. We usually have two rides: a gentle route of about twelve miles and a longer one that’s closer to twenty-five. New members can choose whichever feels comfortable. There’s no pressure to keep up with the faster riders, and the group stops at regular points so nobody gets left behind.
That’s reassuring. Where exactly is the clubhouse? I’ve seen the riverside path, but I don’t know that part of town very well.

We’re at number fourteen Mill Lane. That’s just behind the old library, not the community centre on Bridge Street. The postcode is RG7 4PL. If you’re coming by bike, there are racks in the courtyard. There’s also a bus stop at the end of the lane, though the buses are less frequent in the evening.
Thank you. I’ll make a note of that. And how do I apply? Can I do it over the phone?

I can take your details now, then I’ll email you the application form and payment instructions. Once you’ve filled it in, you can send it back by email or bring a printed copy to the clubhouse. We don’t take card details over the phone, but you can pay online or by bank transfer.
All right. My surname is Hargreaves. That’s H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S. People sometimes write it with an extra ‘a’ after the ‘g’, but there isn’t one.
Thank you. Hargreaves, with one ‘a’ after the ‘h’, then ‘r-g-r-e-a-v-e-s’. I’ve got it. And what’s the best telephone number for you?
It’s 01632 458 271. I’m usually available in the afternoon, but a text message is fine if I miss your call.
I’ll add that. We can send the form by text as well, but the full information is easier to read in an email. What’s your email address?
It’s daniel.hargreaves at mail dot com. I’ll spell the surname there in the same way. Could I start next month, or do I need to wait for a new membership year?

You can join at any time. The annual fee is the same throughout the year, although if you join after the first of October, we can reduce it by a quarter. Since you’re planning to start next month, you’ll pay the standard beginner rate of thirty-four pounds.
Good. I’ll probably come along for the first time on the twelfth of May. Should I arrive before the meeting starts?

Yes, if you can get here by ten past six, one of the ride leaders can introduce you to everyone and check your bike. Please bring a helmet, a working front light and a rear light, and a spare inner tube if you have one.
We can lend you a high-visibility vest.
I’ve got lights and a helmet, but I’ll need to get an inner tube. Do I need to tell you how much cycling I’ve done before?

There’s a short question on the form about your experience, but it’s only so we can suggest a suitable ride. You don’t need to give us a detailed record. Just mention that you’re comfortable cycling on your own and are new to group rides.
That’s easy enough. And if I have any questions after I’ve read the form, should I call this number?

Yes, this is the club office number. We’re here from nine until five on weekdays. If you call outside those hours, leave a message and I’ll get back to you the next working day. I’ll send your information shortly.
Thanks very much, Helen. I’ll look out for the email and hopefully see you on Thursday.
You’re welcome, Daniel. We’ll be looking forward to meeting you. Goodbye.
Goodbye.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Kingsford Botanic Garden. My name's Helen, and before we begin our walk, I'd like to tell you a little about the new greenhouse complex and the changes we've made to the surrounding gardens.

Some of you may have visited Kingsford before, but quite a lot has changed over the past eighteen months. The new greenhouse officially opens to the general public next Monday. We had originally planned to open it this Saturday, but the final safety inspection took slightly longer than expected.

Garden members, however, can come to a special preview on Sunday afternoon. From next week, the greenhouse will be open every day except Tuesday. The rest of the botanic garden remains open seven days a week, so do bear that distinction in mind.

Entry to the outdoor gardens is still free. There was some discussion about charging everyone an additional fee for the greenhouse, but we've decided against that. Instead, greenhouse admission is included in the normal visitor ticket for the main exhibition area.

Children under twelve enter free when accompanied by an adult. A few practical points before we set off. The new visitor centre is immediately on your right as you come through the main gate. That's where you'll find the information desk and lockers.

We used to provide lockers beside the café, but they've been moved because that area became rather crowded. Large bags aren't allowed inside the greenhouse, so please leave them there. The café itself has been extended and now has an outdoor terrace.

Some early publicity said we'd be opening a restaurant as well, but that plan has been postponed. For the moment, the café serves sandwiches, cakes and hot meals at lunchtime. There are toilets beside the visitor centre and another set near the greenhouse exit.

Wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge from the information desk. We recommend booking one in advance at weekends, although on weekdays that's rarely necessary. And for those of you arriving by bicycle, you'll find the new cycle racks just outside the east gate, not in the main car park as shown on some older maps.

Now, today's guided walk lasts about seventy-five minutes. It was originally designed as a ninety-minute tour, but visitors told us they preferred a little free time afterwards. We'll finish at the greenhouse café, where you're welcome to stay for refreshments.

Please keep together as far as possible. Photography is allowed everywhere on our route, including inside the greenhouse, but we do ask you not to use tripods because they can block the narrow paths. Flash photography is permitted, although it isn't really necessary in most areas.

Right, let's start our walk. The first area we'll visit is the Woodland Garden, just beyond these gates. It's particularly attractive in spring, when the ground is covered with bluebells, but what makes it unusual is its collection of plants that thrive in deep shade.

Many visitors assume the most interesting feature is the old oak tree in the centre, but the shade-loving collection is actually what the gardeners want people to notice. After that we'll cross the small stone bridge into the Mediterranean Garden.

This area has rosemary, lavender, olives and several varieties of thyme. You'll probably notice the strong scent before you reach it. The special feature here is the demonstration of plants that can survive long periods with very little water.

That's increasingly important for gardeners dealing with hotter, drier summers. Next comes the Children's Garden. We considered putting a playground there, but instead we've created a sensory trail. Children can touch soft leaves, smell herbs and listen to grasses moving in the wind.

There's also a small pond, but that's fenced off, so the sensory trail is really the main attraction. From there we'll go into the new Tropical House, the largest section of the greenhouse. It's warm and humid, of course, and contains bananas, cacao and several species of orchid.

Look upwards when you enter because the plants we're proudest of are the climbing vines growing across the overhead frames. Some will eventually reach more than fifteen metres in length. The orchid display is beautiful, but it's the vines that are unique to this part of the garden.

Finally, we'll visit the Desert Garden on the southern side of the greenhouse. You'll see plenty of cacti, but the collection isn't limited to them. The most important exhibit is a group of plants that store water in their leaves and stems, including aloes and agaves.

We call these succulents. There's a display about desert animals nearby, but that's temporary and will be removed at the end of the summer. Before we move on, one final reminder: the greenhouse becomes particularly busy between twelve and two, so if you'd like to return later and look around independently, I'd suggest coming after three o'clock.
Now, if everyone's ready, we'll head towards the Woodland Garden.
Thanks for seeing me, Dr Patel. I wanted to check that my seagrass project is focused enough before I start the main fieldwork.
Of course. Last time, you were thinking of comparing several coastal habitats. Have you narrowed that down?

Yes. I realised comparing seagrass, salt marsh and rocky shore communities would be too ambitious. So now I'm concentrating on two seagrass meadows in the bay and looking at what seems to explain differences in their condition.
Good. And which factors are you proposing to investigate?

I made quite a long list initially. I thought about water temperature because that's easy to measure, and I considered boat traffic because one site is close to a marina. But after reading more papers, I think the two factors worth examining properly are nutrient levels and sediment type.

Nutrient enrichment seems strongly linked with algal growth on the leaves, while sediment composition may affect how well the roots establish. I won't ignore boat traffic completely, but I don't think I can measure its impact reliably within this project.
That sounds sensible. Temperature would probably vary too little between your two sites to tell you much anyway.
Right. I was also wondering whether I should make carbon storage the main theme. Seagrass is important for what's called blue carbon, and there are lots of recent articles on that.

It's certainly topical, but measuring carbon storage properly would require sediment cores and laboratory analysis beyond the scope of your current module. You can discuss it in the background, but I'd keep your actual research question centred on meadow condition.
So perhaps: how do environmental differences between two sites influence seagrass condition?
That's close, though 'environmental differences' is still a bit vague. Since you've already identified nutrients and sediment, name those explicitly. It'll make the project easier to design.
Okay. And for condition, I planned to measure leaf length, shoot density and the percentage of leaf surface covered by algae.
Those are all useful. Which one will be your primary indicator?
I assumed leaf length, because it's straightforward.

Straightforward, yes, but leaf length can change naturally with water depth and exposure. Shoot density will give you a more robust measure of how well established the meadow is. Keep leaf length as supporting data.

So shoot density should be the main indicator. That makes sense. I've also been looking at the two possible study sites. Site A is near the river mouth, and Site B is farther along the coast near the marina.
And are they comparable in depth?

Mostly. At first I thought Site B was much deeper, but that was based on an old chart. I visited both last week at low tide, and if I sample along the inner edge of each meadow, the depth difference is quite small.
Good. What sampling method are you considering?

My first idea was to choose quadrats randomly across each meadow. But because the meadows are different sizes, I thought that might produce uneven coverage. So I've changed to systematic sampling along three transects at each site, placing a quadrat every five metres.
Yes, that's more defensible. It also makes it easier for somebody else to repeat your method later.
For the preliminary site visit, I've already checked access and photographed the meadow boundaries. I also tried taking water samples.
Did that go smoothly?
Not entirely. I filled the sample bottles directly beside the shore, and afterwards I realised I may have disturbed the sediment and contaminated them.
That's exactly why a pilot visit is useful. So for that stage, the key lesson is that you need to revise the procedure before collecting your real data.
I'll use a sampling pole next time so I can collect water slightly farther from where I'm standing.
Good. What about your literature review?
I've found plenty on seagrass decline globally, but less on our region. I was worried that meant the review would be weak.

Not necessarily. In fact, that gap is useful. You have enough international studies to establish the mechanisms, and the limited local evidence helps justify your project. I'd say that stage is already giving you a clear rationale for the research.
That's reassuring. For the main field sampling, I was planning to do everything in one day at each site.
I'd avoid that. Weather and tides can change conditions substantially. Repeat the measurements on at least three different dates. That stage needs replication more than anything else.
Three visits to each meadow. I can manage that. Then for laboratory analysis, I was going to measure nitrate and phosphate concentrations myself using the department equipment.
You can, but the phosphate test is quite sensitive. Have you used that equipment before?
Only once in a practical.
Then arrange a session with the lab technician before processing your samples. For the laboratory stage, getting specialist guidance early will save you from producing unreliable results.
I'll book that. And once I've got the measurements, I thought I'd compare the average values between the two sites.

You'll certainly need averages, but don't stop there. The interesting part will be whether nutrient concentrations and sediment characteristics are associated with shoot density. For the data analysis stage, you'll need to look for relationships between variables, not simply describe each site separately.
So correlation analysis, assuming the data are suitable?
Exactly. Check the distribution first and then decide which test is appropriate.
And finally the report. I tend to leave figures until the end, but that usually becomes stressful.

Then change that habit. As soon as the analysis is complete, start producing clear graphs and maps. For the report-writing stage, the priority is to present the findings visually and consistently. Don't spend too much time making them decorative; clarity matters more.

So revise the water-sampling procedure after the pilot visit, use the literature review to establish the rationale, repeat the field sampling on several dates, get technical help with the lab work, examine relationships during analysis, and prepare clear visuals for the report.
Exactly. If you follow that sequence, the project should remain manageable and still give you something meaningful to say about the condition of the two seagrass meadows.

Today I'd like to look at urban beekeeping, a practice which has expanded considerably in many European and North American cities over the last two decades. When people first hear the term, they often imagine hives squeezed into tiny back gardens, but many successful projects actually use rooftops.

These provide secure spaces above street level and are often available on offices, hotels and apartment buildings. Balconies can sometimes work too, although they usually offer less room for inspecting the colonies and storing equipment.

The location of a hive needs more thought than simply finding an unused surface. Bees normally leave the entrance in a fairly direct line, so beekeepers have to consider their flight paths carefully. A hive placed beside a busy doorway, for example, might cause bees and people to cross at head height.
Turning the entrance towards a wall or screen encourages the insects to rise before travelling further, and this greatly reduces unwanted contact with pedestrians.

Cities may seem polluted and therefore unsuitable for bees, yet urban colonies can encounter some advantages compared with colonies in intensively farmed landscapes. In particular, pesticide exposure may be lower where there is relatively little commercial agriculture. That doesn't mean cities are chemical-free, of course; pesticides are still used in parks, private gardens and along railway lines.
However, the variety of flowering plants in urban areas can provide bees with a surprisingly continuous supply of nectar and pollen.

There is, however, an important ecological concern. Honey bees are only one group of pollinating insects, and increasing the number of managed hives can create competition for food. Researchers are especially interested in the effects on wild bees, many of which live alone rather than in large colonies.
So while installing a few hives may support environmental education, putting hundreds into a small district could place additional pressure on existing pollinator populations.

Let's move on to the practical needs of a colony. New beekeepers often concentrate on flowers but forget that bees also require a reliable water source. In the countryside, this may be a pond or stream, whereas in a city bees sometimes discover swimming pools, dripping taps or even air-conditioning systems.
It's far better to provide shallow water close to the hive, ideally with stones or floating material where the insects can land safely.

Food availability also changes throughout the year. People tend to assume that midsummer is the most difficult period because hot weather dries plants out, but in many temperate cities the real challenge comes in early spring. Colonies begin expanding at this time and suddenly need large quantities of pollen, while relatively few plants may yet be flowering.
Tree species such as willow and certain maples can therefore be particularly valuable at the start of the season.

Now, many beginners become interested in keeping bees because they expect to produce large amounts of honey. Honey production can certainly be rewarding, but honey yield varies enormously between sites and from one year to another. Weather is crucial, as are colony health and the amount of forage available.
So a beekeeper shouldn't assume that a hive in a fashionable city-centre garden will automatically produce more than one located on the outskirts.

There are also legal and administrative issues to consider. Regulations vary significantly between cities: some require hive registration, others specify minimum distances from neighbouring properties, and certain buildings ban beekeeping altogether. Another matter that beginners sometimes overlook is public liability.

Even when bees are generally calm, a member of the public could claim to have been injured or suffered an allergic reaction, so appropriate insurance may be advisable or even compulsory in some schemes.

Good relationships with the surrounding community are equally important. Some enthusiastic beekeepers make the mistake of installing colonies first and explaining them afterwards. A better approach is to speak with local residents before the bees arrive, describing where the hives will be positioned and how swarming will be managed.
Offering a short demonstration or sharing a small amount of honey later can also help, but communication at the beginning is more important than giving people gifts.

Finally, urban beekeeping can contribute to research as well as food production. Because hives are distributed across different neighbourhoods, they can provide information about flowering seasons, environmental conditions and changes in insect behaviour. Several universities now involve volunteer beekeepers in citizen science, asking them to record observations using standard methods.
Such projects are useful because professional researchers could never monitor so many locations themselves, although the data still have to be checked carefully for consistency.

So, to summarise, urban beekeeping can have educational, social and scientific value, but simply adding more hives is not automatically beneficial for biodiversity. Successful projects consider the physical site, the needs of the colony, possible effects on other pollinators and the concerns of people living nearby.

With careful planning, bees can become an interesting part of urban life rather than a source of conflict. In our next lecture, we'll examine how city planners can design public green spaces to support a wider range of pollinating insects.
Good afternoon, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like some information about family membership, please. My wife and I have two children, and we'd like to swim together at weekends.
Of course. I'll take a few details so I can fill in the enquiry form. First, can I have your family name?
It's Okafor. O-K-A-F-O-R.
Thank you. And what's the best contact number for you?
It's zero seven seven zero zero nine zero zero one five two. That's my mobile, so it's the best one to ring during the day.
Got it. And how many children will be joining?
Two. Our daughter is nine and our son is six. Both of them can swim a little, but they're not very confident yet.
That's no problem. We have lessons for every level. The family package covers two adults and up to three children under sixteen, so you're well within that. Which day would suit you for swimming?
Saturday would be best, because the children don't have school. Is there a quieter time in the day?
The pool is quietest early in the morning. Most families arrive just before the first lesson. What time would you normally arrive?
We'd aim for half past seven, so we can be in the water by eight.
Half past seven is a good time for a quiet session. The monthly fee for the family package is eighty-four pounds. That includes unlimited swimming and gym access for both adults.
That's reasonable. Does it include lessons for the children?
Lessons are an extra, so the fee only covers access. But I can add the children's course at a reduced rate if you'd like it.
Let's leave that for now. When could we start?
Membership can start on the first of September. If you join before then, the first week is free.
The first of September is perfect. Can we also choose a locker?
Yes, lockers are assigned by number. Which one would you like?
Locker twenty-two, if it's free. It's near the family changing room, which is handy with two children.
Let me check. Yes, twenty-two is available. Now, how would you like to pay?
I'd prefer to pay by direct debit, so the money comes out automatically each month.
No problem. One last question: is there any medical condition we should know about for anyone in the family?
Yes, our son has asthma. He carries an inhaler, and I'd like the lifeguards to know about it.
Thank you, I'll note that on the record, and the lifeguards will be informed. Is there anything else I can help you with?
No, that's everything. Thanks very much.
You're welcome. We'll send you a confirmation by email this evening.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Greenwood Botanical Gardens. My name is Helen, and I'll be your guide for this morning's tour. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a little background and a few practical points, because some of you are new to the gardens and the layout can be a bit confusing at first.

The gardens were originally built in 1880 as a private estate for the Harrington family. They loved plants, and over the years they collected species from all over the world. When the last family member died, the estate was given to the city, and it opened to the public in 1923.
So, as you can see, the gardens still have a very grand, old-fashioned feel in places, especially around the lake.

The tour takes about an hour and a half and covers the four main areas. We'll start at the visitor centre, not at the main gate, so please make sure you've found us before you wander off. The tour begins at ten o'clock sharp, because the glasshouse opens for a short time at the beginning of the morning, and I want to be inside while it's quiet.

Speaking of the glasshouse, which is in the north-west corner of the gardens and a bit of a walk from here, I need to ask you something. It's full of delicate plants, and large bags can knock the leaves and damage the displays.

Could you please leave any large bags in the lockers at the visitor centre? Small handbags and cameras are fine to bring with you. The lockers are free, but they take one pound coins, so please check you have some change.

Now, the most popular part of the tour, especially with children, is the butterfly enclosure. It's a warm, netted area, and there are around forty species flying around at this time of year. Please don't touch the butterflies, and keep the gate closed behind you.
If you're interested in photography, this is the best spot on the whole tour.

After the butterflies, we'll walk down to the lily pond by the lake. The lake is quite deep in the middle, so please keep children close to the path. The pond is home to several species of water lily, and some of them only flower at night, which is a lovely thing to see if you come back in the evening.

You'll find the sensory garden on the way back. It's designed for visitors who are blind or partially sighted, but everyone is welcome to use it. The plants have strong scents and different textures, and there are labels in large print and in braille.
It sits just behind the glasshouse, so we'll pass it on our way to the herb garden.

Finally, the tea room is on the far side of the central lawn, directly opposite the visitor centre. It's a great place to rest your feet at the end of the tour. Most of the cakes are made with herbs from our own herb garden, which is a nice touch.
Please note that the tea room closes at four, while the gardens themselves stay open until six.

Let me finish with a few reminders. The guidebook costs four pounds, but you can borrow a free map at the desk if you don't want to buy anything. We'll finish the tour at the gift shop, which is next to the main gate.
After that you're free to explore on your own. Please meet back at the visitor centre if you want to join the afternoon tour, which starts at quarter past one.
So, to recap: be at the visitor centre for ten o'clock, leave your large bags in the lockers, and keep your eyes open for the water lilies. Does anyone have any questions before we set off?
Hi Dr Walsh, thanks for seeing us. We've started the library project, and we'd like to check our approach before we go any further.
Of course. Let's see where you are. Tell me about the survey first.
We've done one, but I'm not confident in it. We asked only fifty people, and most of them were students who use the building every day.

That's the main problem. Fifty is too small to tell you much, and if the sample is mostly students, the results won't reflect the wider community. You need to reach families, older residents and people who don't use the library at all.
Right, we'll redo it. Tom wants to include a short video of the building in the presentation, to show its current state.
A video can help people picture the place, but it doesn't tell the audience anything new. Something more interactive would work better.
That's what I thought too. I'd like to run a live survey during the presentation, so the audience can vote on the options in real time.
I like that. It makes the presentation engaging, and it gives you immediate feedback. What else are you planning?
We want to compare the costs of the three options.

Yes, definitely. A cost comparison is essential, because the council will want to see value for money. Don't bother with a model of the building, though. It takes ages to make, and your audience won't need it.
Agreed. We won't do a model, and the map of the bus routes isn't relevant either, so we'll leave it out.
Good. Now, the opening hours. You mentioned that the library closes at six. Have you looked at how it's used in the evenings?
Not yet. Our assumption is that evenings are quiet, but we haven't checked.
Then look at the evening use figures before you decide anything. If evening use is high, the case for extending the hours becomes much stronger. Don't rely only on what you think.
OK, we'll do that. We've also walked around the site and made some notes. Shall I go through the problems?
Please. Let's start with the entrance.
The ground floor is the first problem. There's a side entrance, but there's no step-free access there, so wheelchair users have to go round the back.
That's a serious issue, and it should be highlighted. What about upstairs?
The upper floor has plenty of space, but the lighting is too dim for reading. Several people told us they avoid it for that reason.
Lighting is often cheap to fix, so that could be a quick win. What about the outside?
The reading garden is pleasant, but it floods after heavy rain, so it can't be used for much of the winter.
That will be expensive to fix, so present it as a separate option. And the basement?
The basement is the children's area. It's mainly used by parents with pushchairs, and the staff think it should be bigger.
Good. Now, the report. When is the deadline?
It's due on Friday, and we have to submit it online by then.
Remember the word limit. The report must be no more than two thousand words, and the appendices don't count towards it.
Got it. Thanks, that's really helpful.
My pleasure. Send me the revised survey before the weekend, and we'll look at it together.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming. Today's talk is about urban beekeeping, which has grown quickly over the past decade. I'll cover three things: why cities have become attractive for bees, what you need to do before you start, and the practical problems that beekeepers face, especially in the summer months.

Let's start with a point that surprises many people. Cities can actually offer bees more flowers than the countryside does. Modern farmland is often covered by a single crop for much of the year, so bees have very little to feed on.

Parks, gardens and balconies, by contrast, usually contain a wide range of flowering plants, and those flowers keep blooming over a longer season. That is why most of the new hives in our city are in urban areas.

Where do you put the hive? This is one of the first questions beginners ask. Most of the hives in our city are placed on rooftops, because they are out of the way of people and pets. A rooftop also gives the bees a clear flight path.
If you don't have a roof, a secure corner of a large garden can work, as long as the entrance faces away from the path.

Now, the legal side. Before you bring a single colony home, you must register it with the national bee register. The registration is free and takes about ten minutes online, but it is compulsory. The register helps the authorities track disease, and it also means that your neighbours can contact you quickly if a swarm escapes.
Many beginners forget this step, so please don't be one of them.

Let's talk about the bees themselves. A healthy colony in the middle of summer can contain up to sixty thousand bees, and that number can change very quickly. Most of the work is done by the workers, who are all female.
They make the honey, look after the young and guard the entrance. The queen's only job is to lay eggs, so she's not really in charge of anything in the way people imagine.

Foraging is where the real journey happens. Individual bees can travel up to three kilometres from the hive in search of nectar and pollen. That's a long way for an insect that weighs less than a paperclip. In a city, this means that a hive on one side of the river can use gardens on the other side, which is one reason urban honey often has such a complex flavour.

The position of the hive also matters for the bees' health. Hives should face south-east, so they catch the morning sun. That warms the colony early, so the bees can leave the hive sooner, and it also helps to dry out the wet conditions that encourage mould.
Keep the hive away from strong winds, and make sure there is a shallow tray of water nearby, because bees need water to cool the hive in hot weather.

Inspection is the next topic. In the active season, you should check each hive every seven days. A thorough inspection takes time, but it's the only way to spot problems early, such as a queen who has stopped laying or a colony that is preparing to swarm.
Keep a notebook, because it's easy to forget what you saw two weeks ago, and the notes will also help you spot patterns.

Now, the biggest threat. Many beginners expect the weather or the lack of flowers to be the main danger, but in reality it is a parasite called varroa. This mite feeds on the bees and spreads viruses from one colony to another.

If you don't treat it, the colony will usually die within a couple of years. The treatments are straightforward, but you must follow the timing carefully, and you must test regularly to see whether the mite count is rising.

Finally, the reward. A good hive in a productive year can produce around twenty kilograms of honey, although the amount varies enormously from one season to the next. Most urban beekeepers don't sell their honey, they share it with neighbours or give it away.
Some groups also run small projects with schools, which is a lovely way to introduce children to the natural world.

If you'd like to learn more, we run beginners' workshops for new members. They take place at the community centre on Saturday mornings, and they include a hands-on session with a real hive. You don't need any experience, and you don't need to buy any equipment until you've decided that beekeeping is right for you.
Please sign up at the front desk after the talk, and bring a notebook. Thank you for listening, and I'll take questions now.
Good morning, Riverside Student Housing. How can I help you?
Hello. I'm starting a master's course in September, and I'm looking for a flat close to the campus, because I'll be studying in the library late most evenings. My name is Linh Tran. That's T-R-A-N.
Thanks, Linh. Let me note that down. What's the most you can pay each month?
I'd like to keep it at six hundred and fifty pounds a month at most. It would also be good if the bills were included.
We have a few options in that range. Most of our flats include heating and internet in the rent, so there are no surprise bills at the end of the month.
That sounds good. When can I move in?
All our flats are free from the first of September. If you arrive earlier, we can arrange that, but you'd pay for the extra days.
The first of September is fine. I don't have any furniture yet, so I'd like a flat that comes furnished.

All three of the flats I have in mind are furnished, with a desk, a bed and a wardrobe. Let me tell you about them. Oak House is two minutes from the bus stop, which is useful if you don't have a car.
Mill Court is next to a supermarket, so you can buy groceries on the way home. And Garden Lodge is right beside the riverside park, which is lovely in the evenings.
Oak House sounds convenient. Could I see it?
Of course. I've booked you a viewing on Thursday morning at ten. We'll meet at the main reception, so please bring a copy of your acceptance letter from the university.
Perfect. I'll be there. Thank you for your help.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hoi An Ancient Town walking tour. My name is Duc, and I'll be your guide for the next two hours. Please gather around me. We'll meet outside the old post office on Tran Phu Street.
We're starting early this morning to avoid the afternoon heat, so let's keep moving.

A few practical points before we begin. The tour price includes bottled water and entrance tickets to several of the old houses. Please bring a sun hat, because there is very little shade in the open squares, and wear comfortable shoes, since we'll be walking on uneven streets.

Our first stop is the Japanese Covered Bridge. It was built several centuries ago, and it's one of the town's most recognisable landmarks. Please don't rush across it. The best photos are taken from the riverbank anyway.
After that, we'll visit a lantern workshop. Many families here still make handmade lanterns, using bamboo and silk. You'll have about twenty minutes to try making one yourself.
Finally, we'll walk along the old tailors' street. Many of the tailors can make a shirt in one day if you order in the morning, so if you're interested, you can ask them at the end.
One more thing. The night market opens after sunset, so I suggest you come back after the tour ends. The lanterns there look lovely in the evening. Thank you, and let's begin!
Come in, Ben. Let's look at your cycling project. Where have you got to?
Mia and I have decided to compare bike lanes in Amsterdam and Hanoi. We've already got figures on how many people cycle to work in each city.
The trouble is that the accident figures we found only cover 2019, so they might be out of date.
That's a real weakness. Check whether the city councils have published newer figures. Now, what are your options for the presentation itself?
We could show a short video of the bike lanes, run a live survey of the audience, include a map of cycle routes, add a cost comparison, or arrange interviews with city planners.
With only ten minutes, you can't do everything. What have you decided?
The video would take up too much time, and interviews are hard to arrange in just a few weeks. So we think a route map and a cost comparison are the best choices.
Agreed. What about the survey idea?
We thought about asking the audience to vote on which city is safer, but it's probably not worth it.
I'd avoid it. A survey of thirty people won't be representative, so it's risky to draw conclusions from it.
Understood. We'll drop it.
Good. What are you doing next week?
I'll contact the city council to ask for the latest figures. If I can get them by Wednesday, I can update the charts.
Excellent. Can you and Mia write the draft introduction? The draft is due on Friday, and I'll read it over the weekend.
Of course. We'll send it to you on Friday morning.
Let's meet again in room fourteen next Monday to go through the draft.

Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at coral reef restoration. To begin, it's worth knowing how little of the ocean floor is covered by reefs. Coral reefs cover only about one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species.
That's why losing them is such a serious problem.

The biggest threat today is rising sea temperatures. When the water gets too warm, corals lose the algae that give them their colour and their food, and many of them begin to die. Other pressures, such as pollution and overfishing, make recovery even harder.

Restoration projects usually follow two main methods. The first is coral nurseries. Scientists grow small coral fragments in nurseries, often on land or in shallow water, and then transplant them to damaged reefs. The second method is to attach fragments to artificial structures, often made of concrete, which are placed on the seabed.

Early results are encouraging but not perfect. Roughly sixty percent of transplanted fragments survive their first year, which is better than many people expected. However, the survival rate depends heavily on the site and on the water conditions.

One practical rule is that divers should never touch the corals while they work. Even a light touch can damage the tissue, so the teams use special markers to show where each fragment has been placed.
There is also good news about wildlife. In restored areas, fish populations often recover within two years, which tells us the wider ecosystem is responding.
Of course, all of this is expensive. A typical large project can cost about two hundred thousand dollars, and most of that money comes from government grants rather than private companies.
For next semester, the research team plans to use drone surveys to track changes across much larger areas. The results will be published in the spring, so I'd recommend keeping an eye on the journal.
Good morning, Hillside Community Centre. How can I help you?
Hi, I'd like to sign up for the beginners' pottery course I saw advertised.
Of course. Can I take your surname, please?
It's Jensen. That's J-E-N-S-E-N.
Thanks, Laura. The course runs on Wednesdays, but we also have a Thursday evening group if that suits you better.
Thursday would be perfect, I work late on Wednesdays.
Lovely. That class starts at half past six, so six thirty. We only take eight people in each group, so the studio doesn't get crowded.
Is it in the main hall? I went there for a yoga class once.
No, the pottery classes are held in the art studio, behind the library. Just follow the signs from the car park.
Great. And how much is the fee? Does it include materials?

It's forty-five pounds for six weeks. That covers the clay and the firing of your finished pieces. Tools are free to borrow, but you have to pay for a certificate if you'd like one, and refreshments are not included.
That's fine. What will we be making?
In the first week everyone makes a simple mug. The second week is a bowl, and in the third week you'll try a vase, which is the hardest. After that you can choose your own projects.
Sounds good. Should I bring anything?
Just an apron, because the clay gets everywhere. We'll see you next Thursday, then.
